title: Rule vs Learning - Hands-On Exploration (Lab)
summary: Working unplugged at two stations, students run a fixed rule-card machine and a learn-from-examples card game, log the differences and design a test that would reveal which kind an unknown system is.
objectives: Explore a rule-based demo and a simple learning demo and log the differences you observe.
Devise a test that could tell whether a system follows rules or learns.
Predict what would break each system and check your prediction.

body: Today you get your hands on two machines - one that never changes and one that learns from examples. Watch closely: their differences will jump out.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run the rule-card machine and the learn-from-examples game and record what each does.
I can log at least three differences I observed between them.
I can design a fair test that would reveal whether a system follows rules or learns.

terms.definition: A fixed stack of if-then cards that always behaves the same way.
A labelled card the group learns a pattern from.
The rule-of-thumb your group builds from the example cards.
A new input you give a system to see how it behaves.
Behaves the same way every time for the same input.

sections.heading: Two stations, two behaviours
body: At Station A the [[rule-card machine]] never changes. Feed the same input twice and you get the same output twice. That is a rule-based system.
At Station B nobody gives you rules. You study [[example card]]s, build a [[pattern]], then classify new cards. That is a learning system in miniature.

sections.heading: Design a fair test
body: To tell the two apart, give each a brand-new, unusual input. A rule-based machine reacts the same as always or breaks. A learning system tries to match the pattern it built.
The best detectives write down exactly what they will try and what each result would mean.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Run both stations, log the differences, then design a test that would reveal which kind an unknown machine is.
items: Take a role: feeder, recorder or tester.
Run Station A with five inputs, including one strange one.
Run Station B: study examples, then sort five new cards.
Write one test that would separate rules from learning.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which station was more predictable, and how did you know?
What made the learning game guess wrongly?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the clearest difference you saw today.
Write what you would test first on a mystery machine.

worksheet.title: Week 1 - Lab - Worksheet | Rule vs Learning - Hands-On Exploration (Lab)

questions.prompt: Sam is given a mystery machine and wants to find out whether it follows fixed rules or learns. Which test would actually tell him?

options.text: Give it a brand-new, unusual input and watch whether it reacts the same as always or tries to match a pattern.
Give it only inputs it has handled before and check that the answers are still right.
Give it the same easy input five times and time how fast each answer comes back.
Count how many different answers the machine can give altogether.

feedback.correct: Exactly - a new, unusual input is what splits them: fixed rules react the same or break, while a learning system reaches for the pattern it built.
feedback.incorrect: Familiar inputs, speed and the number of answers look much the same for both kinds. Only a brand-new, unusual input shows whether the machine follows a written step or matches a pattern.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to run a fair test on a mystery machine.

items.text: Write down the unusual input you will try and what each possible result would mean.
Give that unusual input to the machine.
Record exactly what the machine did.
Use what you recorded to decide whether the machine follows fixed rules or learns.

feedback.correct: That is how a detective works - decide what each result would mean before you test, so the result can't be bent to fit afterwards.
feedback.incorrect: Plan first: write the input and what each result would mean, then test, then record what happened, and only then decide which kind of machine it is.

questions.prompt: Match each thing a group tried at the two stations with what happened.

left.text: Fed the rule-card machine the same card twice
Fed the rule-card machine a strange card that no rule covered
Gave the card game example cards that were all of one kind
Gave the card game plenty of varied, correctly labelled example cards

right.text: It gave exactly the same output both times.
It stopped, because no step had been written for that card.
The pattern it built came out lopsided and it sorted new cards badly.
The pattern it built sorted most of the new cards correctly.

feedback.correct: Good - each machine fails in its own way: fixed rules break on a case with no rule, and a learning system is only as good as the examples it was shown.
feedback.incorrect: The rule-card machine repeats itself and breaks when no rule fits; the card game's guesses follow the examples it was given, so one-sided examples make a lopsided pattern.

questions.prompt: True or false? A rule-based machine can still fail: if it meets an input that none of its rules covers, it stops or gives a wrong answer.

feedback.correct: Yes - following fixed rules does not mean never failing; it means failing whenever something turns up that has no rule.
feedback.incorrect: Fixed rules are predictable, not perfect. At Station A the strange card had no rule, so the machine stopped or answered wrongly.

questions.prompt: Fill in the gaps. We tested a mystery machine with a brand-new, unusual input, and it gave exactly the answer it always gives, so we decided it ___(1). The Station B card game behaved differently: it tried to match the ___(2) it had built from the example cards.

feedback.correct: That is the difference in one sentence: fixed rules repeat themselves, while a learning system reaches for the pattern it built from its examples.
feedback.incorrect: An unchanged answer to a brand-new input points to fixed rules; the card game instead matched the pattern it had built from the example cards.

formative.targets: Checks whether students can observe and articulate the rule-based vs learning distinction through investigation
formative.check: Comparison log with at least three logged differences and one devised test
formative.successCriteria: Logs at least three real differences and writes a test that would actually separate rules from learning.
formative.evidence: Completed comparison log and the group's devised test.
